summary: This excerpt from Kate Douglas Wiggin's novel (Book 11, part 21) opens with a childish letter from Rebecca to John, mentioning the mortgage on the Simpsons' house and Rebecca's gratitude toward Aunt M. It then describes Rebecca's first week of schooling at Riverboro Centre, where Miss Sawyer arranges her enrollment with teacher Miss Dearborn, and Rebecca's daily walk to school through woods and pastures. The narrator digresses on Miss Dearborn's untrained, instinctive teaching, comparing it to animal behavior.
one_line: Rebecca begins school at Riverboro Centre under Miss Dearborn and walks there through woods and pastures.
key_facts: Rebecca's arrival had been on a Friday, and on the following Monday she began her education at the school in Riverboro Centre, about a mile distant.
Miss Sawyer borrowed a neighbor's horse and wagon to drive Rebecca to the schoolhouse.
Miss Sawyer interviewed the teacher, Miss Dearborn, and arranged for books.
Miss Dearborn had had no special preparation in the art of teaching; it came to her naturally, according to her family.
The narrator compares Miss Dearborn's method to that of Tom Tulliver's clergyman tutor, who acted with 'uniformity of method and independence of circumstances.'
The narrator cites a naturalist's account of a beaver building a dam in a room up three pair of stairs in London.
Rebecca walked to school after the first morning and loved this part of the day's programme.
The short cut ran through the woods when the dew was not too heavy and the weather was fair.
Along the route Rebecca crept through uncle Josh Woodman's bars and waved away Mrs. Carter's cows.
Rebecca jumped from stone to stone across a woodland brook, startling the drowsy frogs.
The 'woodsy bit' featured slippery brown pine needles and fungous growths of brilliant orange and crimson around dead stumps.
Rebecca's letter to John compares herself to the new dog that bit the rope, and says education will be the making of her and help pay off the mortgage when they grow up.
The letter's writer signs off as 'Your loving Becky' and mentions that the Simpsons are mortgaged, though neither Richard Carter nor Dr. Winship is.
